zh: 第四、次明治病方法，行者既安心修道，或本四大有病，因今用心，心息鼓擊，發動成病，或時不能善調適身、息、心三事，內外有所違犯，故有病發。夫坐禪之法，若能善用心者，則四百四病自然差矣。若用心失所，則動四百四病。是故若自行化他，應當善識病源，善知坐中內心治病方法。若不知治病方法，一旦動病，非唯行道有障，則大命有慮。今明治病法中，即為二意：一、明病發相；二、明治病方法。
en: Fourth, next clarifying the methods for treating illness: once the practitioner has settled the mind and taken up cultivation of the path, it may happen that the four elements, already carrying some underlying illness, are struck and stirred by the very application of mind and breath now underway, and illness is thereby brought on; or, at times, the practitioner simply fails to properly regulate the three matters of body, breath, and mind, some fault arising internally or externally, and illness is brought on in this way as well. As for the method of sitting meditation: if one is able to apply the mind skillfully, the four hundred and four illnesses will naturally be cured of themselves; but if the mind is applied improperly, these same four hundred and four illnesses will instead be stirred into motion. Hence, whether practicing for oneself or teaching others, one must properly recognize the source of illness, and properly know the methods for treating illness with the inner mind while sitting. If these methods are unknown, then, once illness is actually stirred up, not only will one's practice of the path be obstructed, but one's very life may be placed in jeopardy. Here, within clarifying illness, there are two parts: clarifying the marks of illness arising; and clarifying the methods of treating illness.

zh: 病發雖復多途，略出不過三種：一者、四大增動病相；二者、從五臟生病；三者、五根中病。略明四大病者，地大增故，腫結沈重，身體枯瘠，如是等百一患生。水大增故，痰癊脹滿，飲食不消，腹痛下利等百一患生。火大增故，煎寒壯熱，支節皆痛，口爽、大小行不通利等百一患生。風大增故，虛懸戰掉，疼痛轉筋，嘔吐嗽氣急，如是等百一患生。故經云：「一大不調，百一病惱；四大不調，四百四病一時俱動。」四大病發，各有相貌，當於坐時及夢中察之，其相眾多，不可具記。
en: Although illness arises through many different paths, in brief, no more than three kinds are given: the marks of illness arising through the four elements' excess and disturbance; illness arising from the five internal organs; and illness within the five faculties.

Clarifying briefly the illnesses of the four elements: when the earth element is in excess, swellings, hardness, and heaviness arise, the body withering and thin — a hundred and one such afflictions arise from this. When the water element is in excess, phlegm and distension arise, food and drink failing to digest, abdominal pain and diarrhea — a hundred and one such afflictions arise from this. When the fire element is in excess, alternating chills and high fever arise, every joint aching, the mouth's sense of taste disordered, urination and defecation obstructed — a hundred and one such afflictions arise from this. When the wind element is in excess, a hollow, unsteady trembling arises, aching pain and cramping, vomiting, coughing, and shortness of breath — a hundred and one such afflictions arise from this. Hence the sūtra says: "When a single element is unregulated, a hundred and one illnesses trouble the body; when all four elements are unregulated, four hundred and four illnesses stir all at once." The illnesses of the four elements each have their own distinct appearance, to be observed both while sitting and in dreams; their marks are manifold and cannot be recorded in full.

zh: 二、次明五臟生患之相：從心生患者，多身體寒熱、口燥等，心主口故；從肺生患者，多身體脹滿、四支煩疼、悶、鼻塞等，肺主鼻故；從肝生患者，多喜愁憂不樂，悲思瞋恚，頭痛、眼痛疼闇等，肝主眼故；從脾生患者，身體面上遊風，通身㿇㿇，痒悶疼痛，飲食失味，脾主舌故；從腎生患者，或咽喉噎塞，腹脹耳滿，腎主耳故。五臟生患眾多，各有其相，於坐時及夢中察之可知。其相眾多（云云），不可具記。
en: Second, next clarifying the marks of illness arising from the five internal organs: illness arising from the heart mostly shows as alternating chills and fever throughout the body, a parched mouth, and the like, since the heart governs the mouth. Illness arising from the lungs mostly shows as distension throughout the body, aching in all four limbs, a feeling of oppression, a stuffed nose, and the like, since the lungs govern the nose. Illness arising from the liver mostly shows as excessive worry, sorrow, and unhappiness, grief and anger, headache, and eye pain or dimness, since the liver governs the eyes. Illness arising from the spleen shows as a wandering, wind-like sensation over the face and body, an all-over numbness, itching, oppression, and pain, and a loss of taste in food and drink, since the spleen governs the tongue. Illness arising from the kidneys shows as, perhaps, a choked, obstructed throat, abdominal distension, and a stuffed feeling in the ears, since the kidneys govern the ears. Illness arising from the five organs is manifold, each with its own distinct mark, to be observed both while sitting and in dreams; their marks are manifold (and so on) and cannot be recorded in full.

zh: 三、次略明五根中患相。身患者，身體卒痛，百節酸疼、瘡痒等。舌患者，瘡強急，飲食失味等。鼻患者，鼻塞甕及流濃涕等。耳患者，耳滿疼聾及或時嘈嘈然作聲等。眼患者，眼懸視𥆨𥆨及瞖闇疼痛等，如是四大、五臟、五根病患，因起非一，病患眾多，不可具說。問曰：五根之患，無異五臟內外相因，今何以別說？答曰：為坐中別有治法故，須別說其相。
en: Third, next briefly clarifying the marks of illness within the five faculties. Illness of the body shows as sudden pain throughout the body, aching in every joint, sores and itching, and the like. Illness of the tongue shows as sores, stiffness, a loss of taste in food and drink, and the like. Illness of the nose shows as a blocked, stuffy nose and thick, flowing mucus, and the like. Illness of the ears shows as a stuffed, aching, or deafened feeling, and, at times, a buzzing sound, and the like. Illness of the eyes shows as a strained, unsteady gaze, and cloudiness, dimness, or pain, and the like. Such illnesses of the four elements, the five organs, and the five faculties arise from more than one cause, and their afflictions are manifold, not to be described in full. Question: are the afflictions of the five faculties not simply the inward-outward counterpart of the five organs' own afflictions — why, then, are they explained separately here? Answer: because there are separate methods for treating them while sitting, their marks must be explained separately.

zh: 行者若欲修禪，脫有患生，應當善自知因，起三種病，通因內外發動。若外傷寒冷熱風，飲食不慎，而病從三處發者，當知因外發。若用心不調，觀行違僻，或內心法起，不知將息，而致此三處病發，此因內發。復次，行者應知得病有三種不同：一者、四大增損故病，如前說；二者、鬼神所作及因魔事觸惱，故得病；三者、業報所得病。如此等病，初得即治，甚易得差；若經久，則病成身羸，治之則為難愈。
en: If the practitioner, wishing to cultivate dhyāna, happens to have illness arise, one should properly recognize its cause oneself. The arising of the three kinds of illness comes about through both external and internal triggers in common. If external injury from cold, chill, heat, or wind, or carelessness with food and drink, causes illness to arise from these three sources, one should know this arises from an external cause. If the mind is applied unevenly, contemplative practice goes astray, or some internal mental dharma arises without one knowing how to properly rest and regulate it, so that illness arises from these same three sources, this arises from an internal cause.

Furthermore, the practitioner should know that falling ill comes about in three differing ways: illness from the excess or deficiency of the four elements, as described above; illness obtained through the actions of spirits or through contact and disturbance from demonic affairs; and illness obtained through karmic retribution. Illnesses such as these, if treated as soon as they first arise, are cured quite easily; but if allowed to persist for a long time, the illness becomes established and the body grows weak, and treatment then becomes difficult to bring to a cure.

The four-elements/five-organs/five-faculties triad gives three overlapping diagnostic lenses on the same body rather than three separate ailments, and the Q&A is explicit about why: the five faculties get their own listing not because they're physiologically distinct from the five organs but because sitting practice has a distinct treatment for each, a reminder that this whole section is organized around what a meditator can actually do about an illness, not around anatomy for its own sake. The three-cause scheme (elemental imbalance, demonic disturbance, karmic retribution) at the end quietly cross-references the previous section's third obstruction (karma) and anticipates the coming chapter on demonic affairs — illness, obstruction, and demons are being treated as three points on a continuum rather than unrelated topics.

zh: 二、正明治病方法者，既深知病源起發，當作方法治之。治病之法，乃有多途，舉要言之，不過五種：一者、氣息治病，所謂六種息及十二種息。何等為六種氣？一、吹；二、呼；三、嘻；四、呵；五、噓；六、呬。此六種息皆於脣口之中方便轉側而作，若於坐時，寒時應吹，熱時應呼。若以治病，吹以去寒，呼以去熱，嘻以去痛，及以治風，呵以去煩，又以下氣。噓以散痰，又以消滿，呬以補勞。若治五臟，呼、吹二氣可以治心，噓以治肝，呵以治肺，嘻以治脾，呬以治腎。
en: Second, directly clarifying the methods of treating illness: once the source of the illness's arising is deeply understood, one should apply the proper method to treat it. The methods for treating illness are themselves manifold; stated in their essentials, they come to no more than five: first, treating illness through the breath, namely the six kinds of therapeutic exhalation and the twelve kinds of therapeutic breath.

What are the six kinds of therapeutic exhalation? Chuī; hū; xī; hē; xū; and xì. These six kinds of exhalation are all made through skillfully shaping the lips and mouth in different ways: while sitting, one should use chuī when cold and hū when hot. As treatments: chuī expels cold; hū expels heat; xī expels pain, and also treats wind; hē expels vexation, and also brings the breath down; xū disperses phlegm, and also relieves distension; and xì replenishes fatigue. As treatments for the five organs: hū and chuī together may treat the heart; xū treats the liver; hē treats the lungs; xī treats the spleen; and xì treats the kidneys.

zh: 復次，有十二種息能治眾患：一、謂上息；二、下息；三、滿息；四、燋息；五、增長息；六、滅壞息；七、暖息；八、冷息；九、衝息；十、持息；十一、和息；十二、補息。此十二息皆心中作想而用。今略明十二息對治患之相。上息治沈重，下息治虛懸，滿息治枯瘠，燋息治腫滿，增長息治損，滅壞息治增，暖息治冷，冷息治熱，衝息治壅結不通，持息治戰動，和息通治四大不和，補息資補四大。善用此息，可以遍治眾患，用之失所，各生眾患，推之可知。諸師用息治病，方法眾多（云云），不備說，今略示一兩條，令知大意。
en: Furthermore: there are twelve kinds of therapeutic breath able to treat every affliction: the rising breath; the sinking breath; the filling breath; the scorching breath; the augmenting breath; the dissolving breath; the warming breath; the cooling breath; the surging breath; the sustaining breath; the harmonizing breath; and the replenishing breath. All twelve of these breaths are applied through visualization within the mind. Here, the mark of each of the twelve breaths' treatment is briefly clarified: the rising breath treats heaviness and sinking; the sinking breath treats a hollow, unsteady feeling; the filling breath treats withering and thinness; the scorching breath treats swelling and distension; the augmenting breath treats depletion; the dissolving breath treats excess; the warming breath treats cold; the cooling breath treats heat; the surging breath treats blockage and obstruction; the sustaining breath treats trembling and shaking; the harmonizing breath treats disharmony among the four elements generally; and the replenishing breath restores and nourishes the four elements. Used skillfully, these breaths are able to treat every affliction universally; used improperly, each in turn gives rise to its own further afflictions — this may be readily understood through reflection. The various masters' methods for treating illness through the breath are themselves manifold (and so on) and are not given here in full; only one or two points are shown here in brief, so that the general sense may be known.

zh: 二、明假想治病者，具如《雜阿含》、《治禪病祕法》七十二法中廣說。但今人神根既鈍，作此觀想，多不成就。或不得其意，非唯治病不差，更增眾患。故諸師善得意者，若有祕要，假想用之，無往不愈，但不可具以文載。三、呪術治病者，萬法悉有對治，以相厭禳，善知其法術，用之無不即愈。呪法出諸修多羅及禪經中，術法諸師祕之，多不妄傳。
en: Second, clarifying treating illness through visualization: this is explained at length in the Saṃyukta Āgama and in the Secret Methods for Treating the Illnesses of Dhyāna, among its seventy-two methods. But since people's spiritual faculties in the present age are already dull, this contemplative visualization is, for the most part, not successfully accomplished; or, failing to grasp its proper sense, not only does it fail to cure the illness, it may increase one's afflictions still further. Hence, among masters who have genuinely grasped its sense, where there is some secret essential, visualization is used and there is nowhere it fails to cure — but this cannot be conveyed in full through writing.

Third, treating illness through mantra: every dharma whatsoever has its own antidote, warded off and dispelled through its corresponding counter-force; one who properly knows this method and its technique, using it, finds nowhere it fails to cure at once. Mantra methods are given in the various sūtras and in the Chan Sūtra; the technique itself is kept secret by the various masters, and, for the most part, is not transmitted carelessly.

zh: 四、用心主境治病者，有師言：「心是一期果報之主，譬如王有所至處，群賊迸散。心王亦爾，隨有病生之處，住心其中，經久不散，病即除滅。」又師云：「用心住憂陀那。此云丹田，去臍下二寸半，多治眾患。」又師云：「安心足下，多有所治。」其要眾多，今不具說。五、觀析治病者，用正智慧檢受病既不可得，四大之患即自消滅。若是鬼神及因魔羅得病，當用強心加呪，及以觀照等法助治之。若是業病，必須助以修福、懺悔、轉讀，患即自滅。
en: Fourth, treating illness by fixing the mind as ruler over its object: one master says: "The mind is the ruler of this present life's own retribution — just as, wherever a king arrives, the surrounding bandits scatter and flee, the mind as ruler is exactly the same: wherever illness has arisen, if the mind is made to dwell there and not disperse for a long while, the illness is thereby removed and extinguished." Another master says: "Fix the mind, dwelling on udāna" — this refers to the cinnabar field, two and a half inches below the navel — "which treats a great many afflictions." Yet another master says: "Settling the mind at the soles of the feet also treats a great many afflictions." The essentials here are themselves manifold, and are not given here in full.

Fifth, treating illness through analytic contemplation: using right wisdom to examine the illness one is undergoing, and finding that it cannot be found at all, the affliction of the four elements is thereby extinguished of itself. If the illness is caused by spirits or by contact with a demon's affairs, one should use a fortified mind together with mantra, and such methods as contemplative illumination, to assist in its treatment. If it is a karmic illness, one must assist its treatment with cultivating merit, repentance, and reciting the sūtras, and the affliction will be extinguished of itself.

zh: 此五種治病之法，若行人善得一意，則可自行兼他，況復具足通達。若都不知其一，則患生無治，非唯廢修正業，亦恐性命有慮，豈可自行教人？是故欲修禪之者，必須善解內心治病之法。內心治病方法眾多，豈可具傳於文？若欲習知，當更尋訪上來所出是旨，是示其大意。若但依此文，文既闕略，恐未可定怙，智者善得其意，方便迴轉，無善知識之處，亦足權以救急。
en: As for these five methods of treating illness: if the practitioner properly grasps even a single one of them, this alone is enough to practice for oneself and assist others as well, let alone were one to master all five completely. But if none of the five is known at all, then, once illness has arisen, there is no way to treat it — not only would this cause one's proper cultivation to be abandoned, it might also place one's very life at risk. How, then, could one practice or teach others without this knowledge? Hence anyone wishing to cultivate dhyāna must properly understand these inner methods of treating illness with the mind. The methods for treating illness with the inner mind are themselves manifold — how could they possibly be conveyed in full through writing? Should one wish to study them properly, one should further seek out the sources cited above; what is given here only indicates their general sense. If one relies on this text alone, the text itself being incomplete, it may not be entirely reliable as a guide — the wise, having properly grasped its sense, will apply it with skillful adaptability; and, in a place with no wise teacher at hand, even this alone is enough to serve as an emergency remedy.

The five methods move from the most externally verifiable (breath, with an audible or visible technique) to the most purely internal (analytic contemplation, which needs no physical component at all), with visualization explicitly flagged as effective in principle but risky in practice for "people's spiritual faculties in the present age," and mantra, by contrast, said to cure at once in every case for one who properly knows its method, though its techniques are kept secret by the masters — a candid admission that a technique's theoretical power doesn't guarantee it suits every practitioner or era. The treatise's own closing caveat is worth taking seriously on its own terms: it says outright that its account is incomplete and that a skilled teacher's live judgment matters more than the text — unusually explicit humility about the limits of a written medical-contemplative manual.

quiz.q: What effect does skillful or improper use of the mind in sitting have on the 404 illnesses?
options: skillful use cures them naturally; improper use stirs them up
quiz.why: "If one is able to apply the mind skillfully, the four hundred and four illnesses will naturally be cured of themselves; but if the mind is applied improperly, these same four hundred and four illnesses will instead be stirred into motion."

quiz.q: In brief, how many kinds of illness-arising are given?
options: three: excess of the four elements, from the five organs, within the five faculties
quiz.why: "Although illness arises through many different paths, in brief, no more than three kinds are given: the marks of illness arising through the four elements' excess and disturbance; illness arising from the five internal organs; and illness within the five faculties."

quiz.q: According to the sūtra cited, how many illnesses arise when one element, or all four, are unregulated?
options: one element: 101 illnesses; all four: 404 at once
quiz.why: "Hence the sūtra says: 'When a single element is unregulated, a hundred and one illnesses trouble the body; when all four elements are unregulated, four hundred and four illnesses stir all at once.'"

quiz.q: Among illnesses of the five organs, what does the liver govern, and what are its symptoms?
options: the mouth; chills and dry mouth
the eyes; worry, sorrow, anger, headache, eye pain or dimness
quiz.why: "Illness arising from the liver mostly shows as excessive worry, sorrow, and unhappiness, grief and anger, headache, and eye pain or dimness, since the liver governs the eyes." The heart governs the mouth, lungs the nose, spleen the tongue, and kidneys the ears.

quiz.q: Since the faculties' illnesses correspond to the organs', why discuss them separately?
options: because sitting practice has distinct treatments, so their marks must be described separately
quiz.why: "Question: are the afflictions of the five faculties not simply the inward-outward counterpart of the five organs' own afflictions — why, then, are they explained separately here? Answer: because there is a distinct treatment method specific to sitting practice."

quiz.q: The text says illness comes about in three different ways. Which?
options: excess or deficiency of the elements, spirits and demonic disturbance, karmic retribution
quiz.why: "Falling ill comes about in three differing ways: illness from the excess or deficiency of the four elements ...; illness obtained through the actions of spirits or through contact and disturbance from demonic affairs; and illness obtained through karmic retribution."

quiz.q: The methods of treating illness, in essentials, are which five?
options: breath, visualization, mantra, fixing the mind as ruler over its object, analytic contemplation
quiz.why: The text gives, in turn, treating illness through the breath, through visualization, through mantra, by fixing the mind as ruler over its object, and through analytic contemplation. Faith, application, and the rest are the ten conditions.

quiz.q: How are the six exhalations used for cold and heat while sitting?
options: chuī when cold, hū when hot
quiz.why: "While sitting, one should use chuī when cold and hū when hot. As treatments: chuī expels cold; hū expels heat."

quiz.q: Treating the five organs with the six exhalations, which treats the lungs?
quiz.why: "As treatments for the five organs: hū and chuī together may treat the heart; xū treats the liver; hē treats the lungs; xī treats the spleen; and xì treats the kidneys."

quiz.q: Among the twelve breaths, what do the rising breath and the sinking breath treat?
options: rising treats heaviness; sinking treats a hollow, unsteady feeling
quiz.why: "The rising breath treats heaviness and sinking; the sinking breath treats a hollow, unsteady feeling; the filling breath treats withering and thinness; the scorching breath treats swelling and distension."

quiz.q: How are the twelve breaths applied?
options: all through visualization within the mind
by shaping the lips and mouth
quiz.why: "All twelve of these breaths are applied through visualization within the mind." The six exhalations are made by shaping the lips and mouth.

quiz.q: What reservation does the text express about treating illness through visualization?
options: people's faculties today are dull, so it mostly fails, or, misunderstood, increases illness
quiz.why: "But since people's spiritual faculties in the present age are already dull, this contemplative visualization is, for the most part, not successfully accomplished; or, failing to grasp its proper sense, not only does it fail to cure the illness, it may increase one's afflictions still further."

quiz.q: In fixing the mind as ruler, where does one master say to fix it, and what is udāna?
options: dwelling on udāna, the cinnabar field, two and a half inches below the navel
quiz.why: "Another master says: 'Fix the mind, dwelling on udāna' — this refers to the cinnabar field, two and a half inches below the navel — 'which treats a great many afflictions.'" Another says the soles of the feet, and another compares the mind to a king before whom bandits scatter.

quiz.q: What is analytic contemplation for illness, and how is karmic illness treated?
options: using right wisdom to find the illness cannot be found, so the elements' ailment ends; karmic illness needs merit, repentance, and recitation
quiz.why: "Treating illness through analytic contemplation: using right wisdom to examine the illness one is undergoing, and finding that it cannot be found at all, the affliction of the four elements is thereby extinguished of itself ... If it is a karmic illness, one must assist its treatment with cultivating merit, repentance, and reciting the sūtras."

quiz.q: What does the text say happens if none of the five treatment methods is known?
options: when illness arises there is no remedy; not only is cultivation abandoned, life itself may be at risk — how could one practice or teach
quiz.why: "But if none of the five is known at all, then, once illness has arisen, there is no way to treat it — not only would this cause one's proper cultivation to be abandoned, it might also place one's very life at risk."
